name: Subnet a Block and Build It
brief:
The U7 mastery gate, end to end. You are given one /24 and four host requirements. Work the plan on paper first, then configure the live network from it and prove every LAN can reach every other LAN.

The block is 192.168.50.0/24. Allocate largest requirement first, starting at the bottom of the block, with no gaps and no overlap:

  LAN-A (PC-A, off R1 G0/0/0) — 60 hosts
  LAN-B (PC-B, off R1 G0/0/1) — 28 hosts
  LAN-C (PC-C, off R2 G0/1)  — 12 hosts
  WAN link R1 to R2          —  2 hosts

Give every LAN its first usable address as the router interface. Put PC-A at .10, PC-B at .70, PC-C at .100. On the WAN link R1 takes the first usable address and R2 the second.
watchFor: The WAN link needs two addresses, not two hundred. If you give it a /24 you have just spent the whole block on one cable. R1 is a 4331, so its interfaces are numbered 0/0/0, 0/0/1, 0/0/2 — platforms differ and the competition will not warn you.

tasks.text: LAN-A: address R1 GigabitEthernet0/0/0 as the gateway and bring it up.
tasks.hint: 60 hosts needs 62 usable, so a /26. First subnet, first usable address: 192.168.50.1 255.255.255.192.

tasks.text: LAN-B: address R1 GigabitEthernet0/0/1 as the gateway and bring it up.
tasks.hint: 28 hosts needs 30 usable, so a /27. LAN-A ended at .63, so LAN-B starts at .64 and its first usable is .65.

tasks.text: LAN-C: address R2 GigabitEthernet0/1 as the gateway and bring it up.
tasks.hint: 12 hosts needs 14 usable, so a /28. LAN-B ended at .95, so LAN-C starts at .96 and its first usable is .97.

tasks.text: WAN link: address R1 GigabitEthernet0/0/2 with the first usable address of a /30.
tasks.hint: Two hosts needs a /30 — mask 255.255.255.252. LAN-C ended at .111, so the WAN is .112/30 and the usable pair is .113 and .114.

tasks.text: WAN link: address R2 GigabitEthernet0/0 with the second usable address.
Address PC-A at .10 with LAN-A mask and gateway.
tasks.hint: Use the IP Configuration panel on PC-A. The mask has to match the subnet, not the class.

tasks.text: Address PC-B at .70 with LAN-B mask and gateway.
Address PC-C at .100 with LAN-C mask and gateway.
On R1, add a route to LAN-C through R2.
On R2, add a default route back to R1. R2 is a stub, so one default beats two specifics.
Run show ip interface brief on both routers and confirm every used interface is up / up.
Prove PC-A can reach PC-B — two LANs on the same router, no static route required.
tasks.hint: Both networks are directly connected to R1, so R1 already knows both. That is what a C route means.

tasks.text: Save the configuration on both routers.

extension: Redo the plan for the same four requirements out of 172.16.8.0/22 instead, and say how many addresses you waste in each case. Then work out how many more LAN-C-sized subnets the leftover space in the /24 would hold.
debrief:
Two things the competition tests here. First, that you size a subnet to the requirement rather than to habit — a /30 on a point-to-point link is not pedantry, it is what leaves room for the rest of the plan. Second, that you can turn a written plan into a working network without a second pass.

Notice PC-A reached PC-B with no static route at all. Two directly connected networks route between each other for free; only LAN-C needed a route, because only LAN-C is on the far side of a router.
